title: C482/790/2017 of Smt. Nirmala Mehta Vs Narendra Singh Mehta AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Misc. Application No. 790 of 2017
Under Section 482 of Cr.P.C.
Smt. Nirmala Mehta ....... Petitioner
Vs.
Narendra Singh Mehta and others ....Respondents
Ms. Meenakshi Parihar, Advocate for the petitioner.
Mr. Siddharth Sah, Advocate for the respondents.

Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J.
Present petition under Section 482 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as "the Code) is filed
by the petitioner against the judgment and order dated 07.04.2017,
passed in Criminal Revision No. 01 of 2017, Narendra Singh Mehta &
others Vs. State of Uttarakhand and another (hereinafter referred to as
"the revision"), by the court of learned Additional Sessions Judge,
Bageshwar. By the impugned judgment and order, the summoning
order dated 06.01.2017, in Criminal Case No. 788 of 2016, Nirmala
Mehta Vs. Narendra Singh Mehta and others (for short "the case")
passed by the court of learned Chief Judicial Magistrate Bageshwar has
been set aside.
2. Briefly stated, on a complaint filed by the petitioner after
inquiry under Section 200 and 202 of the Code, the court of learned
Chief Judicial Magistrate, Bageshwar vide order dated 06.01.2017,
summoned the respondent Narendra Singh, under Section 498A, 504,
506 IPC and Section 3⁄4 Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 (for short "the
Act") and also summoned Trilok Singh Mehta and Smt. Tulsi Devi and
Km. Reena Mehta for the offence under Section 498 and Section 3/4 of
the Act. This order dated 06.01.2017 was challenged in the said
revision, which was allowed and order dated 06.01.2017 passed in the
case was quashed.

2
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner would urge that the
impugned judgment and order is not in accordance with law. First and
foremost, it is argued that the petition under Section 482 of the Code is
maintainable, in view of the principles of law, as laid down by the
Hon'ble Supreme Court, in the case of Prabhu Chawla Vs. State of
Rajasthan and another (2016) 16 SCC 30. In the case of Prabhu Chawla
(supra), the question before the Court was stated in para-2 of the
judgment, which is as hereunder:-
2. While considering all these matters at the SLP
stage, on 5-7-2013, a Division Bench found the impugned
order of the High Court to be against the law stated in
Dhariwal Tobacco Products Ltd. v. State of
Maharashtra4
. In that case the Division Bench concurred
with the proposition of law that availability of alternative
remedy of criminal revision under Section 397 CrPC by
itself cannot be a good ground to dismiss an application
under Section 482 CrPC. But it noticed that a later
Division Bench judgment of this Court in Mohit v. State of
U.P.5 apparently held to the contrary that when an order
under assail is not interlocutory in nature and is amenable
to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court then there
should be a bar in invoking the inherent jurisdiction of the
High Court. In view of such conflict, these cases were
directed to be placed before the Hon'ble Chief Justice for
reference to a larger Bench and that is how the matters are
before this Bench for resolving the conflict."
4. And the answer to it, is in paras 6 and 7, which read as
hereunder:-
"6. In our considered view any attempt to explain
the law further as regards the issue relating to inherent
power of the High Court under Section 482 CrC is
unwarranted. We would simply reiterate that Section 482
begins with a non obstante clause to state:
"482. Saving of inherent powers of High Court.-
Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or affect the
inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as
may be necessary to give effect to any order under this
Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court or
otherwise to secure the ends of justice."
A fortiori, there can be no total ban on the exercise of such
wholesome jurisdiction where, in the words of Krishan
Iyer, J.
"abuse of the process of the court or other extraordinary
situation excites the Court's jurisdiction. The limitation is
self-restraint, nothing more". (Raj Kapoor case8
, SCC
p.48. para 10).
4. (2009) 2 SCC 370: (2009) 1 SCC (Cri.) 806
5. (2013) 7 SCC 789: (2013) 3 SCC (Cri.) 727
8. Raj Kapoor Vs. State: (1980) 1 SCC 43: 1980 SCC (Cri) 72

3
We venture to add a further reason in support.
Since Section 397 CrPC is attracted against all orders
other than interlocutory, a contrary view would limit the
availability of inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC
only to petty interlocutory orders! A situation wholly
unwarranted and undesired.
7. As a sequel, we are constrained to hold that the
Division Bench, particularly in para 28, in Mohit5 in
respect of inherent power of the High Court in Section
482 CrPC does not state the law correctly. We record our
respectful disagreement."
5. In fact, the summoning order dated 06.01.2017, passed in
the case has been set aside on the ground that the petitioner did not file
the list of witnesses, as required under Section 204 (2) of the Code and
the learned revisional court placed reliance upon the principle of law, as
laid down in the case of Mohd. Tahir and others Vs. State of
Uttarakhand and another 2013 (2) UD 208.
6. Heard learned counsel for the petitioner and learned
counsel for the State and perused the record.
7. Learned counsel for the petitioner would urge that the case
of Mohd. Tahir (supra) has been distinct. In that case, in fact,
complainant filed an application, seeking permission to withdraw the
complaint. The complainants did not take any steps, but processes were
issued.
8. Definitely, the instant case is quite a different case. It is
argued that Section 204 (2) is not mandatory, it is directory; even if, list
of witnesses is not filed before summoning order was passed, it's a
defect, which is curable under Section 465 of the Code and the
petitioner may supply list of witnesses any time to the respondents.
9. It may be noted at this stage only that during the pendency
of this petition, it was informed that respondent Trilok Singh Mehta
died, therefore, his name was deleted from the array of parties.
5. Mohit Vs. State of U.P. (2013) 7 SCC 789: (2013) 3 SCC (Cri.) 727

4
10. In support of his contention, learned counsel for the
petitioner placed reliance upon the principles of law, as laid down in the
cases of Pramila Mahesh Shah Vs. Employees' State Insurance, 2002
CriLJ 2454, Abdullah Bhat Vs. Ghulam Mohd. 1972 CriLJ 277, M/s
Raghbir Singh @ Sons Vs. State of Haryana and another 2012 SCC
Online P&H 10774 and also in the case of Noor Khan Vs. State of
Rajasthan, AIR 1964 SC 286.
11. In the case of Pramila Mahesh Shah (supra), Abdullah
Bhat (supra) and Raghbir Singh (supra), it was, inter alia, observed that
the provisions of Section 204 (2) of the Code are not mandatory but
they are directory.
12. In the case of Noor Khan (supra), discussion was made
with regard to Section 207 A (3) and Section 173 (4) of the old CrPC
and it was held that non-compliance of those provisions does not
necessarily, result in vitiating the proceedings. Therefore, learned
counsel for the petitioner would urge that the impugned judgment and
order deserves to be set aside and petition allowed.
13. At the very outset, learned counsel representing the
respondents would fairly submit that insofar as, compliance of Section
204 (2) of the Code is concerned, it may not be termed as mandatory, in
view of settled legal proposition and, mere non compliance of it, may
not be a ground for quashing the summoning order. But learned counsel
would submit that the petition under Section 482 of the Code is not
maintainable, in view of the provisions, as contained under Section 397
(3) of the Code. It is argued that the respondents have availed the
remedy of revision, but it is argued that the petitioner has a remedy of
revision, which she could have availed. Therefore, it is argued that the
law, as laid down, in the case of Prabhu Chawla (supra) does not apply
in the instant case and petition deserves to be dismissed as not
maintainable.

5
14. Insofar as, maintainability of the petition is concerned, as
quoted above, in the case of Prabhu Chawla (supra) Hon'ble Court had
occasion to interpret in between two views, namely, the principles, as
laid down in the case of Dhariwal Tobacco Products Ltd. (supra) and
Mohit (supra), Hon'ble Court upheld the view, as expressed in the case
of Dhariwal Tobacco Products Ltd. (supra). In which, it was, inter alia,
held that availability of alternate remedy to file criminal revision under
Section 397 of the Code, by itself, cannot be a good ground to dismiss
the petition under Section 482 of the Code. This is law. It is not subject
to any factual matrix.
15. In view of the principles of law as laid down in thecase of
Prabhu Chawla (supra), this Court is of the view that the instant
petition is maintainable.
16. The summoning order dated 06.01.2017, passed in the
case has been quashed in the revision, on the ground that list of
witnesses has not been filed, as required under Section 204 (2) of the
Code. This is definitely something a procedural aspect. It may not be
termed as mandatory. It is an irregularity, which is definitely curable.
The petitioner may submit a list of witnesses as and when proceedings
of the case resumes and in turn, it may be supplied to the respondents.
Merely because the list of witnesses had not been filed before
cognizance was taken, the order taking cognizance cannot be quashed.
Therefore, this Court is of the view that impugned order is not in
accordance with law and it deserves to be set aside and petition
allowed.
17. Learned counsel for the respondents would also urge that
in case the petition is allowed, direction may be issued, so that the bail
application of the respondents may be decided by the trial court, as
expeditiously as possible.
18. The petition under Section 482 of the Code is allowed.

6
19. Judgment and order dated 07.04.2017 passed in Criminal
Revision No. 1 of 2017, Narendra Singh Mehta and others Vs. State of
Uttarakhand and others, by the court of learned Additional Sessions
Judge, Bageshwar is set aside.
20. However, if the respondents appear before the trial court
and applies for bail, their bail application may be considered, as
expeditiously as possible, in accordance with law.
21. Let a copy of this judgment be transmitted to the Court
below for compliance.
(Ravindra Maithani, J.)
 05.07.2019 Jitendra
